question: At what blood alcohol level is a Connecticut boat operator, age 21 or older, presumed to be under the influence?
choice_a: A blood alcohol ratio of two-tenths (.20) of one percent
choice_b: There is no defined blood alcohol threshold in Connecticut
choice_c: A blood alcohol ratio of eight-hundredths (.08) of one percent
choice_d: A blood alcohol ratio of five-hundredths (.05) of one percent
explanation: Connecticut law considers a person under the influence of intoxicating liquor while boating if their blood alcohol ratio is .08 of one percent or higher, matching the general national BUI/DUI standard.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Boating Under the Influence (BUI)," p.28

question: What blood alcohol level applies to a Connecticut boat operator under 21 years of age for BUI purposes?
choice_a: The same .08 threshold that applies to adults 21 and over, with no distinct youth standard
choice_b: There is no BUI standard at all for operators under 21
choice_c: A flat zero-tolerance standard of any detectable alcohol whatsoever
choice_d: Two-hundredths (.02) of one percent or more of alcohol by weight
explanation: Connecticut sets a stricter BUI threshold for operators under 21: a blood alcohol ratio of two-hundredths (.02) of one percent or more, well below the .08 standard used for adult operators.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Other Regulations," p.29

question: Even though Connecticut law allows adult recreational marijuana use, how does that law treat operating a boat while under the influence of marijuana?
choice_a: It remains illegal, and Drug Recognition Experts (DREs) are trained to test suspected impaired boat operators for marijuana or other drugs
choice_b: It is fully legal to operate a boat under the influence of marijuana as long as the operator is over 21
choice_c: Marijuana intoxication cannot be tested for by any Connecticut agency
choice_d: Marijuana-impaired boating carries no consequences of any kind
explanation: Connecticut's marijuana legalization law explicitly kept operating a boat while under the influence of marijuana or other drugs illegal; Drug Recognition Experts (DREs) are trained and deployed to evaluate suspected impaired boaters, and operators found over the limit or who refuse a DRE evaluation face boating license suspension upon arrest.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Marijuana Intoxication and Boating," p.28

question: As highlighted in the 2026 Connecticut Boater's Guide, what new consequence links a BUI (boating under the influence) suspension to a driver's motor vehicle license?
choice_a: BUI and DUI offenses are entirely unrelated with no crossover consequences
choice_b: Recently passed legislation mandates reciprocal suspensions -- a BUI certificate suspension automatically triggers a motor vehicle license suspension, and vice versa for a DUI
choice_c: A BUI conviction has never had any effect on a driver's license in Connecticut
choice_d: Only a DUI can affect a boating certificate; a BUI never affects a driver's license
explanation: The 2026 Boater's Guide highlights recently passed legislation mandating reciprocal suspensions for BUI and DUI offenses: suspension of a Connecticut boating certificate automatically results in suspension of the person's motor vehicle license, and a DUI suspension automatically suspends the boating certificate.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, Director's welcome letter, p.5

question: Under Connecticut's rules, what handrail requirement applies before a person may be allowed on the decked-over bow of a powered vessel that is underway?
choice_a: No handrail is ever required regardless of vessel type
choice_b: A handrail is required only on sailboats
choice_c: The bow must be equipped with a handrail encompassing the bow, and all persons on the bow must stay inward of that handrail
choice_d: Riding on a decked-over bow is legal at any time with no equipment required
explanation: No operator of a powered vessel underway may allow anyone on a decked-over bow unless it has a handrail encompassing the bow, with all persons required to stay inward of it; on open, non-decked bows, sitting or standing on the gunwale is prohibited outright.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Riding on Decks or Gunwales," p.25

question: What exception exists to Connecticut's rule against riding on the bow, gunwale, or transom of a powered vessel underway?
choice_a: There is no exception under any circumstance
choice_b: The rule only applies to vessels under 12 feet
choice_c: The rule only applies at night
choice_d: Persons in or on the bow during anchoring, mooring, or docking activities, or while the vessel proceeds at a dead slow speed
explanation: Connecticut's bow/gunwale riding restrictions do not apply to persons in or on the bow of a vessel engaged in anchoring, mooring, or docking activities, or when the vessel is proceeding at a dead slow speed.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Riding on Decks or Gunwales," p.25

question: What must a Connecticut diver display while underwater swimming or diving, and how close may other boaters legally approach?
choice_a: A red flag with a white diagonal stripe, at least 13 inches high and 15 inches long, two-sided; boaters must not come within 100 feet of the flag
choice_b: A blue flag with no size requirement
choice_c: No flag or marker is required for underwater diving in Connecticut
choice_d: A flag is only required for divers under age 18
explanation: Connecticut requires anyone diving or swimming underwater to display a red-and-white diagonal-striped diver-down flag meeting minimum size requirements, and boaters must not come within 100 feet of it; it's also illegal for a diver to surface or swim more than 50 feet from the flag.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Diving and Underwater Operations," p.25

question: How many divers may legally use the same diver-down flag in Connecticut, unless it is displayed from a boat?
choice_c: There is no numeric limit at all
choice_d: Exactly one diver only, with no exceptions
explanation: Connecticut law limits the number of divers using the same diver-down flag to four, unless the flag is displayed from a boat, in which case the number of divers is limited instead by the legal passenger capacity of the boat.
source_note: 2026 CT DEEP Boater's Guide, "Diving and Underwater Operations," p.25

question: What warrantless authority do Connecticut's boating law enforcement officers (Coast Guard, EnCon police, municipal police, marine officers, harbormasters, etc.) have over vessels?
choice_a: They can only issue paper citations by mail after the fact
choice_b: They have no authority to board any vessel under any circumstances
choice_c: They may stop and board boats to check for compliance with federal, state, or local law, or search without a warrant
choice_d: They may only act if a formal complaint has already been filed
explanation: Within their respective jurisdictions, agencies enforcing Connecticut boating law -- including the Coast Guard, state environmental conservation police officers, municipal police, town marine officers, lake patrolmen, and POST-certified harbormasters -- have authority to stop and board boats to check compliance, or to search without a warrant.

question: Is it legal to willfully or negligently obstruct or delay a law enforcement or rescue vessel responding to an emergency call or pursuing a fleeing violator in Connecticut?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the obstruction is unintentional and brief
choice_b: Yes, boaters have no duty to yield to emergency vessels
choice_c: It is only illegal if the obstruction lasts more than one hour
choice_d: No, it is illegal to willfully or negligently obstruct or delay such a vessel
explanation: Connecticut law makes it illegal to willfully or negligently obstruct or delay a law enforcement or rescue vessel that is answering an emergency call or pursuing a fleeing law violator.

question: What can happen to a Connecticut boat operator who is asked to submit to an on-site engine noise test and believed to be exceeding the state's noise limits?
choice_a: Refusing the on-site test results in a $435 fine, and subsequent refusals result in a $535 fine
choice_b: There is no penalty for refusing a noise test
choice_c: Refusal automatically results in permanent boat confiscation
choice_d: Only a verbal warning is given regardless of refusal
explanation: A marine police officer who believes a motorboat exceeds Connecticut's established noise levels may request an on-site test; failing to submit to that test results in a $435 fine, with subsequent refusals to submit resulting in a $535 fine.
